extracted.intended_audience: physicians, medical scientists, and members of a scientific congress / educated readers interested in history and philosophy of medicine
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging the legitimacy, progress, and scientific character of work in medicine, physiology, and pathology; oriented toward historians/philosophers of science and practicing physicians assessing medical theories and research approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of disease/pathology
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever change of structure or function is hurtful belongs to pathology; pathology is the morphology, the physiology, the distribution, the etiology of abnormal life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes harmless 'variations' from morbid states (lesions, poisoning, diseases); notes there is no sharp demarcation between anatomical variation and tumour or between functional modification that at first promotes health and that which passes into disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing variation from disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes that do not noticeably impede the organism are 'variations'; those that impede activity or cause destruction are 'lesions' or 'diseases'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes continuum rather than sharp boundary; classificatory judgment depends on extent and harmfulness of deviation from typical life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathology must be grounded in normal biology
rubrics_metrics.description: There could be no real science of pathology until the science of physiology had reached a degree of perfection; pathology is a branch of biology and depends on understanding normal activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that understanding disease requires knowledge of normal structure and function; historical examples (Harvey, Morgagni, Bichat) show anatomy/physiology underpin pathology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empiricism followed by deduction as scientific method
rubrics_metrics.description: All true science begins with empiricism and strives to pass out of the empirical stage into deduction of empirical facts from more general truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical record-keeping and inductive generalizations (e.g., Asclepeia votive tablets) form the empirical base; mature science then seeks theoretical explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical and histological evidence as tests for medical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate regional anatomy and anatomical/histological post-mortem investigations supply physicians with a clear basis for disease classification and unerring tests of diagnostic accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites progress from Morgagni to histology; underscores the practical value of anatomical knowledge for diagnosis and surgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of animistic/vitalistic explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern physiology opposes animistic hypotheses and seeks physical explanations of vital phenomena or frankly confesses ignorance when none exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques as unscientific attributions of processes to an undefined 'soul' or 'vital principle' (examples: Harvey's sanguine animistic phrasing, Stahlian animism); praises Cartesian program of physical explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of physics and chemistry to physiology
rubrics_metrics.description: The application of the methods and data of physics and chemistry has driven modern progress in physiology; much of modern physiology is applied physics and chemistry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that advances in chemistry and electrical science provided new analytical tools; rebuts claims that applying physical sciences to living phenomena is a 'false principle.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Cell theory as basis for pathology ('cellular pathology')
rubrics_metrics.description: The life of higher animals is the summation of the lives of cell aggregates; the establishment of the cell theory logically leads to a cellular pathology in which diseases are defined as perturbations of cell-life or of coordinative machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Bichat and subsequent development to cells as physiological elements; notes that in organs composed of different tissues, one tissue can be diseased while others remain healthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-fold classification of disease origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Diseases arise either from abnormal states of the physiological units (cells/tissues) or from perturbation of the coordinating and distributive machinery, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses army analogy (each cell a soldier, organs brigades, CNS as headquarters) to illustrate difference between local cellular disease and systemic/coordinative disorders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutics should be founded on physiology and pharmacology
rubrics_metrics.description: Therapeutics rests upon pharmacology, which in turn has no scientific foundation apart from physiology; discovering means to eliminate perturbations depends on physiological understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames therapeutics as introduction of a system of forces competent to eliminate a given perturbation; stresses interdependence of pathology, physiology, and pharmacology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary integration strengthens medical science
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicine's connection with other biological sciences (anatomy, physiology, chemistry, botany, zoology) is historically necessary and has enriched scientific medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: agriculture improving via chemistry and vegetable physiology; modern medicine benefiting from chemistry, physics, and histology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical records and inductive observation as foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Early clinical records (e.g., votive tablets recording symptoms) provided the empirical data from which the earliest inductive generalizations and prognoses of medicine were based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the role of sustained observation and classification in forming early pathology as natural history of disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution that precise diagnosis may not ensure correct treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: While precise diagnosis is valuable, extensive anatomical/physiological knowledge may prevent doing wrong more than it helps to do right in therapy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes a practicing physician's lament: knowing exactly what is happening does not always translate into effective remedies; implies therapeutic efficacy is a separate standard beyond diagnostic precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about simple mechanistic metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: The living body is better analogized to an army of coordinated units than to a watch or hydraulic machine; purely Cartesian mechanical analogies are incomplete because local vital properties and developmental processes matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues mechanical metaphors that posit a central source of power are misleading; cites Wolff, Hunter, Trembley as showing limits of strict iatro-mechanical explanations.
